text.p: The following are some of the leading stories in Finnish papers this morning.
- If European economic and monetary union (EMU) is weak, Finland should stay outside to preserve its strong economy, says MP Erkki Tuomioja, chairman of the Socialist parliament group.
- Finnish Centre Party should hold extra EMU party conference already in early September, says Kyosti Virrankoski, European Parliament Centre Party representative. @
- Lawyers' fees have not fallen back since the banking crisis court cases of the early 1990s: hourly fee can amount to over 1000 markka.
- Finland and Israel signed an agreement on regular air traffic; Finnish carrier company Finnair does not have plans to open a direct flight line to Israel, company says.
- European Commission's plans to cut farm support are outrageous; market prices do not even cover direct farming expenses, Finnish farmers say. @
- Service station competition in St Petersburg is tightening -- in response, Neste plans to invest in good location and image, company's St Petersburg sales director says.
- Medicine costs could be cut by 200 million markka through cheaper generic medicines, Social and Health Ministry says.
- Restructuring of regional administration and process of decentralisation has increased decision-making powers of Finnish local authorities considerably, an administration study shows. @

- The whole EMU transition is unclear and if timetable is delayed it will become a central issue in Finnish and German elections, Finnish European Parliament representative Paavo Vayrynen says adding that Finland should stay outside of EMU.

- European Union cooperation in foreign policy erodes president's authority and president will become a symbolic figure, says Sirkka-Liisa Anntila, European Parliament representative and deputy chariman of Centre Party.
- German President Roman Hertzog and his wife visited various cultural events on unofficial visit to Finland. @
- More emphasis should be put on Baltic Sea's environmental protection and agricultural emissions should be restricted, Environment Minister Pekka Haavisto says.
